# wasmtime_types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasmtime-types/

## Expand description

Internal dependency of Wasmtime and Cranelift that defines types for WebAssembly.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [wasmparser](https://docs.rs/wasmparser/0.217.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasmparser/index.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Rust module prelude for Wasmtime crates.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [wasm_](https://docs.rs/macro.wasm_unsupported.html)- unsupported
- Return an `Err(WasmError::Unsupported(msg))`where`msg`the string built by calling`format!`on the arguments to this macro.

# anyhow - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/anyhow/^1.0.22/

## Expand description

This library provides [ anyhow::Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html), a trait object based error
type for easy idiomatic error handling in Rust applications.

[§](https://docs.rs#details)Details

-
Use `Result<T, anyhow::Error>`, or equivalently`anyhow::Result<T>`, as the return type of any fallible function.Within the function, use `?`to easily propagate any error that implements the`std::error::Error``use anyhow::Result; fn get_cluster_info() -> Result<ClusterMap> { let config = std::fs::read_to_string("cluster.json")?; let map: ClusterMap = serde_json::from_str(&config)?; Ok(map) }`
-
Attach context to help the person troubleshooting the error understand where things went wrong. A low-level error like “No such file or directory” can be annoying to debug without more context about what higher level step the application was in the middle of. `use anyhow::{Context, Result}; fn main() -> Result<()> { ... it.detach().context("Failed to detach the important thing")?; let content = std::fs::read(path) .with_context(|| format!("Failed to read instrs from {}", path))?; ... }``Error: Failed to read instrs from ./path/to/instrs.json Caused by: No such file or directory (os error 2)`
-
Downcasting is supported and can be by value, by shared reference, or by mutable reference as needed. `// If the error was caused by redaction, then return a // tombstone instead of the content. match root_cause.downcast_ref::<DataStoreError>() { Some(DataStoreError::Censored(_)) => Ok(Poll::Ready(REDACTED_CONTENT)), None => Err(error), }`
-
If using Rust ≥ 1.65, a backtrace is captured and printed with the error if the underlying error type does not already provide its own. In order to see backtraces, they must be enabled through the environment variables described in `std::backtrace`- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
`RUST_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only errors to have backtraces, set `RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only panics to have backtraces, set `RUST_BACKTRACE=1`and`RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=0`.

- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
-
Anyhow works with any error type that has an impl of `std::error::Error`, including ones defined in your crate. We do not bundle a`derive(Error)`macro but you can write the impls yourself or use a standalone macro like[thiserror](https://github.com/dtolnay/thiserror).`use thiserror::Error; #[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum FormatError { #[error("Invalid header (expected {expected:?}, got {found:?})")] InvalidHeader { expected: String, found: String, }, #[error("Missing attribute: {0}")] MissingAttribute(String), }`
-
One-off error messages can be constructed using the `anyhow!`macro, which supports string interpolation and produces an`anyhow::Error`.`return Err(anyhow!("Missing attribute: {}", missing));`A `bail!`macro is provided as a shorthand for the same early return.`bail!("Missing attribute: {}", missing);`

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

In no_std mode, almost all of the same API is available and works the same way. To depend on Anyhow in no_std mode, disable our default enabled “std” feature in Cargo.toml. A global allocator is required.

```
[dependencies]
anyhow = { version = "1.0", default-features = false }
```
With versions of Rust older than 1.81, no_std mode may require an additional
`.map_err(Error::msg)` when working with a non-Anyhow error type inside a
function that returns Anyhow’s error type, as the trait that `?`-based error
conversions are defined by is only available in std in those old versions.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [anyhow](https://docs.rs/macro.anyhow.html)as format_err;

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [anyhow](https://docs.rs/macro.anyhow.html)
- Construct an ad-hoc error from a string or existing non-`anyhow`error value.
- [bail](https://docs.rs/macro.bail.html)
- Return early with an error.
- [ensure](https://docs.rs/macro.ensure.html)
- Return early with an error if a condition is not satisfied.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Chain](https://docs.rs/struct.Chain.html)
- Iterator of a chain of source errors.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- The `Error`type, a wrapper around a dynamic error type.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Context](https://docs.rs/trait.Context.html)
- Provides the `context`method for`Result`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [Ok](https://docs.rs/fn.Ok.html)
- Equivalent to `Ok::<_, anyhow::Error>(value)`.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- `Result<T, Error>`

# cranelift_entity - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cranelift-entity/^0.112.3/

## Expand description

Array-based data structures using densely numbered entity references as mapping keys.

This crate defines a number of data structures based on arrays. The arrays are not indexed by
`usize` as usual, but by *entity references* which are integers wrapped in new-types. This has
a couple advantages:

- Improved type safety. The various map and set types accept a specific key type, so there is no confusion about the meaning of an array index, as there is with plain arrays.
- Smaller indexes. The normal `usize`index is often 64 bits which is way too large for most purposes. The entity reference types can be smaller, allowing for more compact data structures.

The `EntityRef` trait should be implemented by types to be used as indexed. The `entity_impl!`
macro provides convenient defaults for types wrapping `u32` which is common.

- `PrimaryMap`
- `SecondaryMap`
- `SparseMap`
- `EntitySet`
- `EntityList`- `Vec`.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- Compact representation of`Option<T>`for types with a reserved value.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- Macro which provides the common implementation of a 32-bit entity reference.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- A slice mapping`K -> V`allocating dense entity references.
- A small list of entity references allocated from a pool.
- A set of`K`for densely indexed entity references.
- Iterate over all keys in order.
- Iterator type returned by`iter_entity_range`.
- Iterate over all keys in order.
- Iterate over all keys in order.
- A memory pool for storing lists of`T`.
- A primary mapping`K -> V`allocating dense entity references.
- A mapping`K -> V`for densely indexed entity references.
- A sparse mapping of entity references.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- A type wrapping a small integer index should implement`EntityRef`so it can be used as the key of an`SecondaryMap`or`SparseMap`.
- Trait for extracting keys from values stored in a`SparseMap`.
- Helper trait used to add`unsigned()`methods to primitive signed integer types.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- Iterate over a`Range<E: EntityRef>`, yielding a sequence of`E`items.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- A sparse set of entity references.

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0.188/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any - `docsrs`
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Deserialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Serialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.

# smallvec 1.15.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/smallvec/^1.6.1/

docs.rs failed to build smallvec-1.15.2

Please check the

See

If you believe this is docs.rs' fault,

Please check the

[build logs](https://docs.rs/crate/smallvec/1.15.2/builds)for more information.See

[Builds](https://docs.rs/about/builds)for ideas on how to fix a failed build, or[Metadata](https://docs.rs/about/metadata)for how to configure docs.rs builds.If you believe this is docs.rs' fault,

[open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose).# rust-smallvec

"Small vector" optimization for Rust: store up to a small number of items on the stack

## Example

```
use ;

// This SmallVec can hold up to 4 items on the stack:
let mut v:  = smallvec!;
// It will automatically move its contents to the heap if
// contains more than four items:
v.push;
// SmallVec points to a slice, so you can use normal slice
// indexing and other methods to access its contents:
v = v + v;
v.sort;
```

# wasmparser - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasmparser/^0.217.0/

## Expand description

A simple event-driven library for parsing WebAssembly binary files (or streams).

The parser library reports events as they happen and only stores parsing information for a brief period of time, making it very fast and memory-efficient. The event-driven model, however, has some drawbacks. If you need random access to the entire WebAssembly data-structure, this is not the right library for you. You could however, build such a data-structure using this library.

To get started, create a [ Parser](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html) using

[and then follow the examples documented for](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html#method.new)

`Parser::new`[or](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html#method.parse)

`Parser::parse`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html#method.parse_all)

`Parser::parse_all`## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [collections](https://docs.rs/collections/index.html)- `validate`
- Type definitions for maps and sets used by the `wasmparser`crate.
- [names](https://docs.rs/names/index.html)- `validate`
- Definitions of name-related helpers and newtypes, primarily for the component model.
- [types](https://docs.rs/types/index.html)- `validate`
- Types relating to type information provided by validation.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [for_](https://docs.rs/macro.for_each_operator.html)- each_ - operator
- A helper macro to conveniently iterate over all opcodes recognized by this
crate. This can be used to work with either the `Operator``VisitOperator`

# wasmtime_types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wasmtime-types/latest/target-redirect/wasmtime_types/

## Expand description

Internal dependency of Wasmtime and Cranelift that defines types for WebAssembly.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [wasmparser](https://docs.rs/wasmparser/0.217.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasmparser/index.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Rust module prelude for Wasmtime crates.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Badges

Source: https://docs.rs/about/badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

---

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# wasmparser - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasmparser/0.217.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasmparser/index.html

## Expand description

A simple event-driven library for parsing WebAssembly binary files (or streams).

The parser library reports events as they happen and only stores parsing information for a brief period of time, making it very fast and memory-efficient. The event-driven model, however, has some drawbacks. If you need random access to the entire WebAssembly data-structure, this is not the right library for you. You could however, build such a data-structure using this library.

To get started, create a [ Parser](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html) using

[and then follow the examples documented for](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html#method.new)

`Parser::new`[or](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html#method.parse)

`Parser::parse`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html#method.parse_all)

`Parser::parse_all`## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [collections](https://docs.rs/collections/index.html)- `validate`
- Type definitions for maps and sets used by the `wasmparser`crate.
- [names](https://docs.rs/names/index.html)- `validate`
- Definitions of name-related helpers and newtypes, primarily for the component model.
- [types](https://docs.rs/types/index.html)- `validate`
- Types relating to type information provided by validation.

# pyde_events_macros - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pyde-events-macros/0.1.0-alpha.7/pyde_events_macros/

## Expand description

`pyde-events-macros` — backing crate for `pyde::declare_events!()`.

Re-exported from `pyde-host`; contracts never depend on this crate
directly. The function-like macro reads `otigen.toml` at compile
time, parses every `[events.NAME]` block, computes the canonical
topic-0 hash (`Blake3(signature)`) for each, and emits a typed
struct + `emit()` impl under `mod events`. Authors write

and the macro expands into the equivalent
`pyde::emit_event(&[TOPIC0, from, to], &borsh::to_vec(&amount).unwrap())`
call — same wire bytes as a hand-rolled emission, but the topic-0
hash + indexed-topic layout + data encoding are all derived from
`otigen.toml` so a typo at any layer is a compile error.

[§](https://docs.rs#expansion-shape)Expansion shape

For an `otigen.toml` `[events.Transfer]` block like

```
[events.Transfer]
signature = "Transfer(address,address,uint128)"
fields = [
    { name = "from",   type = "address",  indexed = true },
    { name = "to",     type = "address",  indexed = true },
    { name = "amount", type = "uint128" },
]
```
the macro emits roughly

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
pub mod events {
    pub struct Transfer {
        pub from: ::pyde_host::Address,
        pub to: ::pyde_host::Address,
        pub amount: u128,
    }
    impl Transfer {
        pub const TOPIC_0: ::pyde_host::Hash32 = [0x71, 0xfb, /* ... */];
        pub fn emit(&self) {
            let topics = [Self::TOPIC_0, self.from, self.to];
            let data = self.amount.to_le_bytes();
            ::pyde_host::emit_event(&topics, &data);
        }
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#restrictions-in-v1)Restrictions in v1

- Indexed fields must be `address`,`hash32`, or`bytes32`(the 32-byte fixed-width types). Hashing a variable-width indexed value to fit it into a 32-byte topic is a separate convention the chain doesn’t yet pick a side on.
- Non-indexed fields support all primitives (`u8`..`u128`,`i8`..`i128`,`bool`,`address`,`hash32`,`bytes32`,`bytes`,`string`). Multiple non-indexed fields are encoded as a borsh tuple in declaration order.
- Max 4 topics (chain limit, see `HOST_FN_ABI_SPEC`§7.5). With topic[0] reserved for the signature hash, that leaves 3 indexed fields max per event.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [declare_](https://docs.rs/macro.declare_events.html)- events
- `declare_events!()`— read otigen.toml at compile time, emit- `mod events`. Takes no arguments.

# fakecloud_dsql - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fakecloud-dsql/0.31.0/fakecloud_dsql/

## Expand description

AWS Aurora DSQL (`dsql`) restJson1 control-plane service for fakecloud.

Batch 1: the full 16-operation control plane from the AWS Smithy model –
cluster lifecycle (Create/Get/Update/Delete/ListClusters), resource-based
cluster policies (Put/Get/DeleteClusterPolicy), change streams
(Create/Get/Delete/ListStreams), the VPC endpoint service-name lookup, and
tagging (Tag/Untag/ListTagsForResource). Every operation is backed by real,
account-partitioned, persisted state with AWS-shaped identifiers (26-char
lowercase cluster ids, `arn:aws:dsql:...:cluster/<id>` ARNs), an async
CREATING -> ACTIVE / DELETING -> DELETED lifecycle, `clientToken`
idempotency, deletion-protection enforcement, and multi-region property
round-tripping.

The Postgres-compatible data plane (a real container the cluster endpoint resolves to, reachable with an IAM-derived connection token) lands in a follow-up batch; this batch establishes the control plane and full non-code surface. Unimplemented behavior returns a faithful modeled error, never a stub success.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use service::`- [DsqlService](https://docs.rs/service/struct.DsqlService.html);
- `pub use state::`- [DsqlState](https://docs.rs/state/struct.DsqlState.html);
- `pub use state::`- [DSQL_SNAPSHOT_SCHEMA_VERSION](https://docs.rs/state/constant.DSQL_SNAPSHOT_SCHEMA_VERSION.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [persistence](https://docs.rs/persistence/index.html)
- Snapshot save/load helpers for the DSQL control-plane state.
- [service](https://docs.rs/service/index.html)
- Aurora DSQL restJson1 control-plane dispatch and operation handlers.
- [state](https://docs.rs/state/index.html)
- Account-partitioned, serializable state for the Aurora DSQL control plane.
- [ticker](https://docs.rs/ticker/index.html)
- Background lifecycle advancement for DSQL clusters and streams.

# fakecloud_ses - Rust

- DKIM signing for outbound email.

- SES event fanout: publishes send/delivery/bounce/complaint events to configured event destinations (SNS topics, EventBridge buses).

- Hand-rolled RFC 5322 / MIME builder for fakecloud SES.

- Minimal SMTP client used as an opt-in outbound relay for SES
SendEmail / SendEmailV2 / SendRawEmail. Wired only when the
`FAKECLOUD_SES_SMTP_RELAY`env var is set (e.g.`smtp://localhost:1025`to drop mail at a local Mailpit / MailHog instance for development).
- [v1](https://docs.rs/v1/index.html)
- SES v1 Query protocol handlers for identity management, sending, templates, configuration sets, receipt rules, receipt filters, and inbound email processing.

- One email accepted by the inbound SMTP listener
(`ses_smtp.rs::store_email`). Captured alongside the matching`SentEmail`so tests can assert SMTP-specific facts (auth user, raw size) without re-deriving them from`raw_data`.

# theater_handler_message_server - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/theater-handler-message-server/0.3.13/theater_handler_message_server/

## Expand description

Theater Message Server Handler

Provides actor-to-actor messaging capabilities including:

- One-way send messages
- Request-response patterns
- Bidirectional channels

[§](https://docs.rs#todo-messaging-address-refactor)TODO: Messaging Address Refactor

Currently this handler uses `TheaterId` (the runtime’s internal actor identifier)
for message addressing. This is problematic because:

- TheaterId is a runtime concept - it’s generated when spawning actors and is non-deterministic (uses UUIDs)
- Using TheaterId for messaging couples the actor’s identity to runtime internals
- This breaks chain reproducibility - the same actor run twice gets different IDs, so message addresses in the chain differ

The messaging system should have its own address concept that is:

- Separate from the runtime’s internal actor tracking
- Configurable/deterministic (e.g., from manifest config)
- Part of the actor’s “world” rather than runtime internals

This would allow:

- Actors to have stable, reproducible addresses
- Chain events to be deterministic
- Clear separation between runtime bookkeeping and actor behavior

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [events](https://docs.rs/events/index.html)
- Message server handler event types

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Channel](https://docs.rs/struct.ChannelAccept.html)- Accept
- Channel acceptance response
- [Message](https://docs.rs/struct.MessageRouter.html)- Router
- High-throughput message router using channel-based architecture (no locks!)
- [Message](https://docs.rs/struct.MessageServerHandler.html)- Server - Handler
- Per-actor MessageServerHandler that provides actor-to-actor communication.

# pyde_storage_macros - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pyde-storage-macros/0.1.0-alpha.7/pyde_storage_macros/

## Expand description

`pyde-storage-macros` — backing crate for `pyde::declare_storage!()`.

Re-exported from `pyde-host`; contracts never depend on this crate
directly. The function-like macro reads `otigen.toml` at compile
time, parses the `[state]` schema, and emits a `mod storage` with
one typed accessor per field. Authors write

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
pyde::declare_storage!();
#[pyde::entry]
fn deposit(amount: u128) {
    let from = /* ... */;
    storage::balances().write(&from, amount);
}
```
and the macro expands into the equivalent `unsafe { pyde::sstore_map1(...) }`
call against the typed-storage host fns. The chain side
validates field name + value type + key arity + key types and
derives the slot internally (`Poseidon2(self_address || field_name || keys...)`), so the macro is purely a typing + DX layer over an
already-secure substrate.

[§](https://docs.rs#expansion-shape)Expansion shape

For an otigen.toml `[state]` block like

```
[state]
schema = [
    { name = "counter",   type = "uint64" },
    { name = "balances",  type = "map",
      keys = ["address"], value = "uint128" },
    { name = "allowances", type = "map",
      keys = ["address", "address"], value = "uint128" },
]
```
the macro emits roughly

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
pub mod storage {
    pub struct CounterField;
    impl CounterField {
        const FIELD: &'static [u8] = b"counter";
        pub fn read(&self) -> u64 { ... }
        pub fn write(&self, value: u64) { ... }
        pub fn delete(&self) { ... }
    }
    pub fn counter() -> CounterField { CounterField }
    pub struct BalancesField;
    impl BalancesField {
        const FIELD: &'static [u8] = b"balances";
        pub fn read(&self, k1: &::pyde_host::Address) -> u128 { ... }
        pub fn write(&self, k1: &::pyde_host::Address, value: u128) { ... }
        pub fn delete(&self, k1: &::pyde_host::Address) { ... }
    }
    pub fn balances() -> BalancesField { BalancesField }
    // ... etc
}
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [declare_](https://docs.rs/macro.declare_storage.html)- storage
- `declare_storage!()`— read otigen.toml at compile time, emit- `mod storage`.

# pyde_entry_macros - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pyde-entry-macros/0.1.0-alpha.7/pyde_entry_macros/

## Expand description

`#[pyde::entry]` — wraps a Rust function in the calldata-decode +
return-wrap shim required by Pyde’s `() -> ()` entry ABI.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-the-macro-does)What the macro does

Pyde entry points are `() -> ()` at the WASM-function-boundary level
(HOST_FN_ABI §3.5.2). Args flow through the `pyde::calldata_*` host
fns; return data flows through `pyde::return`. Authors who write a
natural Rust signature like `fn deposit(amount: u128, to: Address) -> Receipt` would have to hand-write that decode + return shim per
function. This macro generates it.

[§](https://docs.rs#expansion-shape)Expansion shape

Given:

the macro emits:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[no_mangle]
pub extern "C" fn transfer() {
    fn __pyde_entry_transfer_inner(to: Address, amount: u128) -> bool {
        // ... business logic
        true
    }
    let __pyde_size = unsafe { ::pyde_host::raw::calldata_size() } as usize;
    let mut __pyde_buf = ::alloc::vec![0u8; __pyde_size];
    if __pyde_size > 0 {
        unsafe {
            ::pyde_host::raw::calldata_copy(0, __pyde_size as i32, __pyde_buf.as_mut_ptr());
        }
    }
    let (to, amount): (Address, u128) =
        ::borsh::BorshDeserialize::try_from_slice(&__pyde_buf)
            .expect("calldata decode");
    let __pyde_result = __pyde_entry_transfer_inner(to, amount);
    let __pyde_bytes =
        ::borsh::to_vec(&__pyde_result).expect("encode return");
    unsafe {
        ::pyde_host::raw::pyde_return(__pyde_bytes.as_ptr(), __pyde_bytes.len() as i32)
    };
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#attributes-belong-in-otigentoml-not-on-the-macro)Attributes belong in `otigen.toml`, NOT on the macro

`view`, `payable`, `reentrant`, `constructor`, `fallback`,
`receive`, `sponsored` — all of these are semantic attributes the
chain enforces by reading the deployed `pyde.abi` custom section.
That section is built from the per-function blocks in
`otigen.toml`:

```
[functions.get]
attributes = ["entry", "view"]
```
The macro itself does **not** accept attribute arguments. Passing
any is a compile error pointing the author at `otigen.toml`. The
single source of truth dodges the divergence footgun where the
Rust source claims one thing and the deployed ABI says another.

[§](https://docs.rs#author-requirements)Author requirements

The contract crate must depend on `pyde-host` (which re-exports
this macro) and `borsh`. `pyde-host`’s default features pull in a
global allocator (`dlmalloc`) so `Vec` works inside `#![no_std]`.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [entry](https://docs.rs/attr.entry.html)
- Wrap a function with the Pyde entry-point shim.

# hanzo-kernel 0.2.9 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/hanzo-kernel/0.2.9

Please check the

[build logs](https://docs.rs/crate/hanzo-kernel/0.2.9/builds)for more information.

See

[Builds](https://docs.rs/about/builds)for ideas on how to fix a failed build, or

[Metadata](https://docs.rs/about/metadata)for how to configure docs.rs builds.

If you believe this is docs.rs' fault,

[open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose).

hanzo-kernel: Hanzo's first-party GPU kernel DSL.

Write a kernel ONCE in Rust; it lowers to CUDA / ROCm / Vulkan / Metal. This crate is the
first-party facade over the CubeCL lowering engine: kernel source names only `hanzo_kernel::*`,
never `cubecl`. "Values, not places" -- CubeCL is the implementation value; `hanzo_kernel` is the
stable namespace we build against, so the engine can be upgraded (or forked) without touching a
single kernel.

The perf primitives our hand-tuned kernels rely on are all here and lower to the native instruction on each backend:

- `dot`on a vectorized- `Line<i8>`-> dp4a / OpSDotAccSat (int8 4-way dot)
- `cmma`-> tensor cores (WMMA / cooperative-matrix / simdgroup)
- `SharedMemory`,- `plane_*`(subgroup reduce/shuffle),- `Atomic`, barriers

MIGRATION POLICY (perf-gated, never a downgrade): the DSL provides COVERAGE -- every quant type on every backend, from one source, killing the "same op, N impls, N numeric behaviors" bug class. A hand-tuned kernel is replaced by its DSL twin ONLY when the DSL version is bit-exact AND within perf noise (bench-gated). Where a hand-tuned kernel still wins, it stays as the specialized peak path and the DSL is the portable fallback for the backends that lack a tuned version.

---

# context_governor - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/context-governor/0.1.0/context_governor/

## Expand description

Crate-agnostic governed context compaction for AI agents.

`context-governor` does not call an LLM and does not pretend to extend a
provider’s hard context window. It allocates a limited prompt budget across
agent conversation messages, preserves high-risk context verbatim, demotes or
summarizes low-risk context, emits receipts, and keeps exact fallback ranges
for later expansion.

# tokenfuse - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tokenfuse/0.3.0/tokenfuse/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#tokenfuse)TokenFuse

**Runtime cost control & security for AI agents** — a drop-in proxy between
your agent and its LLM/tool providers that enforces per-run budgets, detects
runaway loops, offers a kill-switch, and keeps secrets out of the model’s
context.

This is the project’s **umbrella crate**. TokenFuse runs as a service, not a
library dependency: the gateway ships as the `tokenfuse` binary and as Docker
images on GHCR.

`docker run -p 4100:4100 -e TOKENFUSE_MODE=enforce ghcr.io/taipanbox/tokenfuse`Point your provider client at `http://127.0.0.1:4100` and attach a few
`X-Fuse-*` headers. See the [repository](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/tokenfuse) for the full documentation, the HA
cluster, the hosted Cloud, and the MCP credential-broker.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_GATEWAY.html)- GATEWAY
- Default gateway address the proxy listens on.
- [VERSION](https://docs.rs/constant.VERSION.html)
- The released TokenFuse version this crate documents.

# rsclaw-plugin 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rsclaw-plugin/0.1.0

[open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose).Plugin subsystem.

Plugins are directories under `~/.rsclaw/plugins/<name>/` with a
`plugin.json5` (or legacy `openclaw.plugin.json`) manifest.

Supported runtimes:

- `node`/- `bun`/- `deno`— JS runtime (subprocess JSON-RPC)
- `wasm`— wasmtime component model

Public API:

- `PluginManifest`/- `load_manifest()`/- `scan_plugins()`
- `SlotRegistry`— memory + context_engine slots
- `Plugin`— live JS plugin handle (spawned subprocess)
- `WasmPlugin`— live WASM plugin handle (wasmtime)
- `load_all_plugins()`— unified loader that dispatches by runtime

- [Wasm](https://docs.rs/struct.WasmRecGroup.html)- RecGroup
- A recursive type group.
- [Wasm](https://docs.rs/struct.WasmRefType.html)- RefType
- WebAssembly reference type – equivalent of `wasmparser`’s RefType
- [Wasm](https://docs.rs/struct.WasmStructType.html)- Struct - Type
- A concrete struct type.
- [Wasm](https://docs.rs/struct.WasmSubType.html)- SubType
- A concrete, user-defined (or host-defined) Wasm type.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [ConstOp](https://docs.rs/enum.ConstOp.html)
- The subset of Wasm opcodes that are constant.
- [Engine](https://docs.rs/enum.EngineOrModuleTypeIndex.html)- OrModule - Type - Index
- An interned type index, either at the module or engine level.
- [Entity](https://docs.rs/enum.EntityIndex.html)- Index
- An index of an entity.
- [Entity](https://docs.rs/enum.EntityType.html)- Type
- A type of an item in a wasm module where an item is typically something that can be exported.
- [Wasm](https://docs.rs/enum.WasmCompositeType.html)- Composite - Type
- A function, array, or struct type.
- [Wasm](https://docs.rs/enum.WasmError.html)- Error
- A WebAssembly translation error.
- [Wasm](https://docs.rs/enum.WasmHeapTopType.html)- Heap - TopType
- A top heap type.
- [Wasm](https://docs.rs/enum.WasmHeapType.html)- Heap - Type
- WebAssembly heap type – equivalent of `wasmparser`’s HeapType
- [Wasm](https://docs.rs/enum.WasmStorageType.html)- Storage - Type
- Represents storage types introduced in the GC spec for array and struct fields.
- [Wasm](https://docs.rs/enum.WasmValType.html)- ValType
- WebAssembly value type – equivalent of `wasmparser::ValType`.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [WASM32_](https://docs.rs/constant.WASM32_MAX_SIZE.html)- MAX_ - SIZE
- Maximum size, in bytes, of 32-bit memories (4G)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- Helpers used to convert a `wasmparser`type to a type in this crate.

# wasmtime_types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasmtime-types/25.0.3/wasmtime_types/index.html

## Expand description

Internal dependency of Wasmtime and Cranelift that defines types for WebAssembly.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [wasmparser](https://docs.rs/wasmparser/0.217.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasmparser/index.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Rust module prelude for Wasmtime crates.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [wasm_](https://docs.rs/macro.wasm_unsupported.html)- unsupported
- Return an `Err(WasmError::Unsupported(msg))`where`msg`the string built by calling`format!`on the arguments to this macro.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Const](https://docs.rs/struct.ConstExpr.html)- Expr
- A constant expression.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataIndex.html)- Index
- Index type of a passive data segment inside the WebAssembly module.
- [Defined](https://docs.rs/struct.DefinedFuncIndex.html)- Func - Index
- Index type of a defined function inside the WebAssembly module.
- [Defined](https://docs.rs/struct.DefinedGlobalIndex.html)- Global - Index
- Index type of a defined global inside the WebAssembly module.
- [Defined](https://docs.rs/struct.DefinedMemoryIndex.html)- Memory - Index
- Index type of a defined memory inside the WebAssembly module.

- Index type of a defined table inside the WebAssembly module.

- Index type of a passive element segment inside the WebAssembly module.
- [Engine](https://docs.rs/struct.EngineInternedRecGroupIndex.html)- Interned - RecGroup - Index
- Index type of a canonicalized recursive type group inside the whole engine (as opposed to canonicalized within just a single Wasm module).

- Index type of a function (imported or defined) inside the WebAssembly module.

- [Module](https://docs.rs/struct.ModuleInternedTypeIndex.html)- Interned - Type - Index

- [Owned](https://docs.rs/struct.OwnedMemoryIndex.html)- Memory - Index

- [RecGroup](https://docs.rs/struct.RecGroupRelativeTypeIndex.html)- Relative - Type - Index

[27](#27)pub trait TypeTrace {
[30](#30)    fn trace<F, E>(&self, func: &mut F) -> Result<(), E>
[34](#34)    where
[35](#35)        F: FnMut(EngineOrModuleTypeIndex) -> Result<(), E>;
[36](#36)
[37](#37)    fn trace_mut<F, E>(&mut self, func: &mut F) -> Result<(), E>
[43](#43)    where
[44](#44)        F: FnMut(&mut EngineOrModuleTypeIndex) -> Result<(), E>;
[45](#45)
[46](#46)    fn trace_engine_indices<F, E>(&self, func: &mut F) -> Result<(), E>
[48](#48)    where
[49](#49)        F: FnMut(VMSharedTypeIndex) -> Result<(), E>,
[50](#50)    {
[51](#51)        self.trace(&mut |idx| match idx {
[52](#52)            EngineOrModuleTypeIndex::Engine(idx) => func(idx),
[53](#53)            EngineOrModuleTypeIndex::Module(_) | EngineOrModuleTypeIndex::RecGroup(_) => Ok(()),
[54](#54)        })
[55](#55)    }
[56](#56)
[57](#57)    fn canonicalize_for_runtime_usage<F>(&mut self, module_to_engine: &mut F)
[68](#68)    where
[69](#69)        F: FnMut(ModuleInternedTypeIndex) -> VMSharedTypeIndex,
[70](#70)    {
[71](#71)        self.trace_mut::<_, ()>(&mut |idx| match idx {
[72](#72)            EngineOrModuleTypeIndex::Engine(_) => Ok(()),
[73](#73)            EngineOrModuleTypeIndex::Module(module_index) => {
[74](#74)                let engine_index = module_to_engine(*module_index);
[75](#75)                *idx = EngineOrModuleTypeIndex::Engine(engine_index);
[76](#76)                Ok(())
[77](#77)            }
[78](#78)            EngineOrModuleTypeIndex::RecGroup(_) => {
[79](#79)                panic!("should not already be canonicalized for hash consing")
[80](#80)            }
[81](#81)        })
[82](#82)        .unwrap()
[83](#83)    }
[84](#84)
[85](#85)    fn is_canonicalized_for_runtime_usage(&self) -> bool {
[87](#87)        self.trace(&mut |idx| match idx {
[88](#88)            EngineOrModuleTypeIndex::Engine(_) => Ok(()),
[89](#89)            EngineOrModuleTypeIndex::Module(_) | EngineOrModuleTypeIndex::RecGroup(_) => Err(()),
[90](#90)        })
[91](#91)        .is_ok()
[92](#92)    }
[93](#93)
[94](#94)    fn canonicalize_for_hash_consing<F>(
[105](#105)        &mut self,
[106](#106)        rec_group_range: Range<ModuleInternedTypeIndex>,
[107](#107)        module_to_engine: &mut F,
[108](#108)    ) where
[109](#109)        F: FnMut(ModuleInternedTypeIndex) -> VMSharedTypeIndex,
[110](#110)    {
[111](#111)        self.trace_mut::<_, ()>(&mut |idx| match *idx {
[112](#112)            EngineOrModuleTypeIndex::Engine(_) => Ok(()),
[113](#113)            EngineOrModuleTypeIndex::Module(module_index) => {
[114](#114)                *idx = if rec_group_range.start <= module_index {
[115](#115)                    debug_assert!(module_index < rec_group_range.end);
[118](#118)                    let relative = module_index.as_u32() - rec_group_range.start.as_u32();
[119](#119)                    let relative = RecGroupRelativeTypeIndex::from_u32(relative);
[120](#120)                    EngineOrModuleTypeIndex::RecGroup(relative)
[121](#121)                } else {
[122](#122)                    debug_assert!(module_index < rec_group_range.start);
[125](#125)                    EngineOrModuleTypeIndex::Engine(module_to_engine(module_index))
[126](#126)                };
[127](#127)                Ok(())
[128](#128)            }
[129](#129)            EngineOrModuleTypeIndex::RecGroup(_) => {
[130](#130)                panic!("should not already be canonicalized for hash consing")
[131](#131)            }
[132](#132)        })
[133](#133)        .unwrap()
[134](#134)    }
[135](#135)
[136](#136)    fn is_canonicalized_for_hash_consing(&self) -> bool {
[138](#138)        self.trace(&mut |idx| match idx {
[139](#139)            EngineOrModuleTypeIndex::Engine(_) | EngineOrModuleTypeIndex::RecGroup(_) => Ok(()),
[140](#140)            EngineOrModuleTypeIndex::Module(_) => Err(()),
[141](#141)        })
[142](#142)        .is_ok()
[143](#143)    }

[291](#291)    }

[298](#298)            Self::EXTERNREF => write!(f, "externref"),
[299](#299)            _ => {
[300](#300)                if self.nullable {
[301](#301)                    write!(f, "(ref null {})", self.heap_type)
[302](#302)                } else {

[304](#304)                }
[305](#305)            }
[306](#306)        }
[307](#307)    }

[500](#500)impl WasmHeapType {
[501](#501)    #[inline]
[503](#503)    pub fn is_vmgcref_type(&self) -> bool {
[504](#504)        match self.top() {
[505](#505)            WasmHeapTopType::Any | WasmHeapTopType::Extern => true,
[508](#508)
[509](#509)            WasmHeapTopType::Func => false,
[511](#511)        }
[512](#512)    }
[513](#513)
[514](#514)    #[inline]
[520](#520)    pub fn is_vmgcref_type_and_not_i31(&self) -> bool {
[521](#521)        self.is_vmgcref_type() && *self != Self::I31
[522](#522)    }
[523](#523)
[524](#524)    #[inline]
[526](#526)    pub fn top(&self) -> WasmHeapTopType {
[527](#527)        match self {
[528](#528)            WasmHeapType::Extern | WasmHeapType::NoExtern => WasmHeapTopType::Extern,
[529](#529)
[530](#530)            WasmHeapType::Func | WasmHeapType::ConcreteFunc(_) | WasmHeapType::NoFunc => {
[531](#531)                WasmHeapTopType::Func
[532](#532)            }
[533](#533)
[534](#534)            WasmHeapType::Any
[535](#535)            | WasmHeapType::Eq
[536](#536)            | WasmHeapType::I31
[537](#537)            | WasmHeapType::Array
[538](#538)            | WasmHeapType::ConcreteArray(_)
[539](#539)            | WasmHeapType::Struct
[540](#540)            | WasmHeapType::ConcreteStruct(_)
[541](#541)            | WasmHeapType::None => WasmHeapTopType::Any,
[542](#542)        }
[543](#543)    }
[544](#544)}

[557](#557)#[derive(Debug, Clone, Eq, PartialEq, Hash, Serialize, Deserialize)]
[559](#559)pub struct WasmFuncType {
[560](#560)    params: Box<[WasmValType]>,
[561](#561)    non_i31_gc_ref_params_count: usize,
[562](#562)    returns: Box<[WasmValType]>,
[563](#563)    non_i31_gc_ref_returns_count: usize,
[564](#564)}
[565](#565)
[566](#566)impl fmt::Display for WasmFuncType {
[567](#567)    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
[568](#568)        write!(f, "(func")?;
[569](#569)        if !self.params.is_empty() {
[570](#570)            write!(f, " (param")?;
[571](#571)            for p in self.params.iter() {
[572](#572)                write!(f, " {p}")?;
[573](#573)            }
[574](#574)            write!(f, ")")?;
[575](#575)        }
[576](#576)        if !self.returns.is_empty() {
[577](#577)            write!(f, " (result")?;
[578](#578)            for r in self.returns.iter() {
[579](#579)                write!(f, " {r}")?;
[580](#580)            }
[581](#581)            write!(f, ")")?;
[582](#582)        }
[583](#583)        write!(f, ")")
[584](#584)    }
[585](#585)}
[586](#586)
[587](#587)impl TypeTrace for WasmFuncType {
[588](#588)    fn trace<F, E>(&self, func: &mut F) -> Result<(), E>
[589](#589)    where
[590](#590)        F: FnMut(EngineOrModuleTypeIndex) -> Result<(), E>,
[591](#591)    {
[592](#592)        for p in self.params.iter() {
[593](#593)            p.trace(func)?;
[594](#594)        }
[595](#595)        for r in self.returns.iter() {
[596](#596)            r.trace(func)?;
[597](#597)        }
[598](#598)        Ok(())
[599](#599)    }
[600](#600)
[601](#601)    fn trace_mut<F, E>(&mut self, func: &mut F) -> Result<(), E>
[602](#602)    where
[603](#603)        F: FnMut(&mut EngineOrModuleTypeIndex) -> Result<(), E>,
[604](#604)    {
[605](#605)        for p in self.params.iter_mut() {
[606](#606)            p.trace_mut(func)?;
[607](#607)        }
[608](#608)        for r in self.returns.iter_mut() {
[609](#609)            r.trace_mut(func)?;
[610](#610)        }
[611](#611)        Ok(())
[612](#612)    }
[613](#613)}
[614](#614)
[615](#615)impl WasmFuncType {
[616](#616)    #[inline]
[617](#617)    pub fn new(params: Box<[WasmValType]>, returns: Box<[WasmValType]>) -> Self {
[618](#618)        let non_i31_gc_ref_params_count = params
[619](#619)            .iter()
[620](#620)            .filter(|p| p.is_vmgcref_type_and_not_i31())
[621](#621)            .count();
[622](#622)        let non_i31_gc_ref_returns_count = returns
[623](#623)            .iter()
[624](#624)            .filter(|r| r.is_vmgcref_type_and_not_i31())
[625](#625)            .count();
[626](#626)        WasmFuncType {
[627](#627)            params,
[628](#628)            non_i31_gc_ref_params_count,
[629](#629)            returns,
[630](#630)            non_i31_gc_ref_returns_count,
[631](#631)        }
[632](#632)    }
[633](#633)
[634](#634)    #[inline]
[636](#636)    pub fn params(&self) -> &[WasmValType] {
[637](#637)        &self.params
[638](#638)    }
[639](#639)
[640](#640)    #[inline]
[642](#642)    pub fn non_i31_gc_ref_params_count(&self) -> usize {
[643](#643)        self.non_i31_gc_ref_params_count
[644](#644)    }
[645](#645)
[646](#646)    #[inline]
[648](#648)    pub fn returns(&self) -> &[WasmValType] {
[649](#649)        &self.returns
[650](#650)    }
[651](#651)
[652](#652)    #[inline]
[654](#654)    pub fn non_i31_gc_ref_returns_count(&self) -> usize {
[655](#655)        self.non_i31_gc_ref_returns_count
[656](#656)    }
[657](#657)
[658](#658)    pub fn is_trampoline_type(&self) -> bool {
[660](#660)        self.params().iter().all(|p| *p == p.trampoline_type())
[661](#661)            && self.returns().iter().all(|r| *r == r.trampoline_type())
[662](#662)    }
[663](#663)
[664](#664)    pub fn trampoline_type(&self) -> Cow<'_, Self> {
[690](#690)        if self.is_trampoline_type() {
[691](#691)            return Cow::Borrowed(self);
[692](#692)        }
[693](#693)
[694](#694)        Cow::Owned(Self::new(
[695](#695)            self.params().iter().map(|p| p.trampoline_type()).collect(),
[696](#696)            self.returns().iter().map(|r| r.trampoline_type()).collect(),
[697](#697)        ))
[698](#698)    }
[699](#699)}

[1385](#1385)#[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq, Hash, Serialize, Deserialize)]
[1389](#1389)pub struct ConstExpr {
[1390](#1390)    ops: SmallVec<[ConstOp; 2]>,
[1391](#1391)}
[1392](#1392)
[1393](#1393)impl ConstExpr {
[1394](#1394)    pub fn new(ops: impl IntoIterator<Item = ConstOp>) -> Self {
[1400](#1400)        let ops = ops.into_iter().collect::<SmallVec<[ConstOp; 2]>>();
[1401](#1401)        assert!(!ops.is_empty());
[1402](#1402)        ConstExpr { ops }
[1403](#1403)    }
[1404](#1404)
[1405](#1405)    pub fn from_wasmparser(
[1410](#1410)        expr: wasmparser::ConstExpr<'_>,
[1411](#1411)    ) -> WasmResult<(Self, SmallVec<[FuncIndex; 1]>)> {
[1412](#1412)        let mut iter = expr
[1413](#1413)            .get_operators_reader()
[1414](#1414)            .into_iter_with_offsets()
[1415](#1415)            .peekable();
[1416](#1416)
[1417](#1417)        let mut ops = SmallVec::<[ConstOp; 2]>::new();
[1418](#1418)        let mut escaped = SmallVec::<[FuncIndex; 1]>::new();
[1419](#1419)        while let Some(res) = iter.next() {
[1420](#1420)            let (op, offset) = res?;
[1421](#1421)
[1422](#1422)            if matches!(op, wasmparser::Operator::End) && iter.peek().is_none() {
[1426](#1426)                break;
[1427](#1427)            }
[1428](#1428)
[1429](#1429)            if let wasmparser::Operator::RefFunc { function_index } = &op {
[1432](#1432)                escaped.push(FuncIndex::from_u32(*function_index));
[1433](#1433)            }
[1434](#1434)
[1435](#1435)            ops.push(ConstOp::from_wasmparser(op, offset)?);
[1436](#1436)        }
[1437](#1437)        Ok((Self { ops }, escaped))
[1438](#1438)    }
[1439](#1439)
[1440](#1440)    pub fn ops(&self) -> &[ConstOp] {
[1442](#1442)        &self.ops
[1443](#1443)    }
[1444](#1444)
[1445](#1445)    pub fn provably_nonzero_i32(&self) -> bool {
[1455](#1455)        assert!(self.ops.len() > 0);
[1456](#1456)        if self.ops.len() > 1 {
[1457](#1457)            return false;
[1460](#1460)        }
[1461](#1461)        match self.ops[0] {
[1463](#1463)            ConstOp::I32Const(0) => false,
[1465](#1465)            ConstOp::I32Const(_) => true,
[1468](#1468)            _ => false,
[1470](#1470)        }
[1471](#1471)    }
[1472](#1472)}
[1473](#1473)
[1474](#1474)#[allow(missing_docs)]
[1476](#1476)#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, Eq, PartialEq, Hash, Serialize, Deserialize)]
[1477](#1477)pub enum ConstOp {
[1478](#1478)    I32Const(i32),
[1479](#1479)    I64Const(i64),
[1480](#1480)    F32Const(u32),
[1481](#1481)    F64Const(u64),
[1482](#1482)    V128Const(u128),
[1483](#1483)    GlobalGet(GlobalIndex),
[1484](#1484)    RefI31,
[1485](#1485)    RefNull,
[1486](#1486)    RefFunc(FuncIndex),
[1487](#1487)    I32Add,
[1488](#1488)    I32Sub,
[1489](#1489)    I32Mul,
[1490](#1490)    I64Add,
[1491](#1491)    I64Sub,
[1492](#1492)    I64Mul,
[1493](#1493)}
[1494](#1494)
[1495](#1495)impl ConstOp {
[1496](#1496)    pub fn from_wasmparser(op: wasmparser::Operator<'_>, offset: usize) -> WasmResult<Self> {
[1498](#1498)        use wasmparser::Operator as O;
[1499](#1499)        Ok(match op {
[1500](#1500)            O::I32Const { value } => Self::I32Const(value),
[1501](#1501)            O::I64Const { value } => Self::I64Const(value),
[1502](#1502)            O::F32Const { value } => Self::F32Const(value.bits()),
[1503](#1503)            O::F64Const { value } => Self::F64Const(value.bits()),
[1504](#1504)            O::V128Const { value } => Self::V128Const(u128::from_le_bytes(*value.bytes())),
[1505](#1505)            O::RefNull { hty: _ } => Self::RefNull,
[1506](#1506)            O::RefFunc { function_index } => Self::RefFunc(FuncIndex::from_u32(function_index)),
[1507](#1507)            O::GlobalGet { global_index } => Self::GlobalGet(GlobalIndex::from_u32(global_index)),
[1508](#1508)            O::RefI31 => Self::RefI31,
[1509](#1509)            O::I32Add => Self::I32Add,
[1510](#1510)            O::I32Sub => Self::I32Sub,
[1511](#1511)            O::I32Mul => Self::I32Mul,
[1512](#1512)            O::I64Add => Self::I64Add,
[1513](#1513)            O::I64Sub => Self::I64Sub,
[1514](#1514)            O::I64Mul => Self::I64Mul,
[1515](#1515)            op => {
[1516](#1516)                return Err(wasm_unsupported!(
[1517](#1517)                    "unsupported opcode in const expression at offset {offset:#x}: {op:?}",
[1518](#1518)                ));
[1519](#1519)            }
[1520](#1520)        })
[1521](#1521)    }

[1606](#1606)    pub fn maximum_byte_size(&self) -> Result<u64, SizeOverflow> {
[1621](#1621)        match self.maximum {
[1622](#1622)            Some(max) => max.checked_mul(self.page_size()).ok_or(SizeOverflow),
[1623](#1623)            None => {
[1624](#1624)                let min = self.minimum_byte_size()?;
[1625](#1625)                Ok(min.max(self.max_size_based_on_index_type()))

[1801](#1801)            wasmparser::ValType::F64 => WasmValType::F64,
[1802](#1802)            wasmparser::ValType::V128 => WasmValType::V128,
[1803](#1803)            wasmparser::ValType::Ref(t) => WasmValType::Ref(self.convert_ref_type(t)),
[1804](#1804)        }

[1819](#1819)            wasmparser::HeapType::Abstract { ty, shared: false } => match ty {
[1820](#1820)                wasmparser::AbstractHeapType::Extern => WasmHeapType::Extern,
[1821](#1821)                wasmparser::AbstractHeapType::NoExtern => WasmHeapType::NoExtern,

[1823](#1823)                wasmparser::AbstractHeapType::NoFunc => WasmHeapType::NoFunc,
[1824](#1824)                wasmparser::AbstractHeapType::Any => WasmHeapType::Any,
[1825](#1825)                wasmparser::AbstractHeapType::Eq => WasmHeapType::Eq,
[1826](#1826)                wasmparser::AbstractHeapType::I31 => WasmHeapType::I31,
[1827](#1827)                wasmparser::AbstractHeapType::Array => WasmHeapType::Array,
[1828](#1828)                wasmparser::AbstractHeapType::Struct => WasmHeapType::Struct,
[1829](#1829)                wasmparser::AbstractHeapType::None => WasmHeapType::None,
[1830](#1830)
[1831](#1831)                wasmparser::AbstractHeapType::Exn | wasmparser::AbstractHeapType::NoExn => {
[1832](#1832)                    unimplemented!("unsupported heap type {ty:?}");
[1833](#1833)                }
[1834](#1834)            },
[1835](#1835)            _ => unimplemented!("unsupported heap type {ty:?}"),
[1836](#1836)        }
[1837](#1837)    }

# wasmtime_types::prelude - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasmtime-types/25.0.3/wasmtime_types/prelude/index.html

## Expand description

Rust module prelude for Wasmtime crates.

Wasmtime crates that use `no_std` use `core::prelude::*` by default which
does not include `alloc`-related functionality such as `String` and `Vec`.
To have similar ergonomics to `std` and additionally group up some common
functionality this module is intended to be imported at the top of all
modules with:

Externally for crates that depend on `wasmtime-types` they should have this
in the root of the crate:

and then `use crate::*` works as usual.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [vec](https://docs.rs/vec/index.html)
- A contiguous growable array type with heap-allocated contents, written
`Vec<T>`.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [format](https://docs.rs/macro.format.html)
- Creates a `String`using interpolation of runtime expressions.
- [vec](https://docs.rs/macro.vec.html)
- Creates a `Vec`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Box](https://docs.rs/struct.Box.html)
- A pointer type that uniquely owns a heap allocation of type `T`.
- [Index](https://docs.rs/struct.IndexMap.html)- Map
- A hash table where the iteration order of the key-value pairs is independent of the hash values of the keys.
- [Index](https://docs.rs/struct.IndexSet.html)- Set
- A default set of values.
- [String](https://docs.rs/struct.String.html)
- A UTF-8–encoded, growable string.
- [Vec](https://docs.rs/struct.Vec.html)
- A contiguous growable array type, written as `Vec<T>`, short for ‘vector’.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Err2](https://docs.rs/trait.Err2Anyhow.html)- Anyhow
- Convenience trait for converting `Result<T, E>`into`anyhow::Result<T>`
- [Into](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoAnyhow.html)- Anyhow
- Convenience trait to convert a value into `anyhow::Error`
- [ToOwned](https://docs.rs/trait.ToOwned.html)
- A generalization of `Clone`to borrowed data.
- [ToString](https://docs.rs/trait.ToString.html)
- A trait for converting a value to a `String`.

---

# wasm_unsupported in wasmtime_types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasmtime-types/25.0.3/wasmtime_types/macro.wasm_unsupported.html

```
macro_rules! wasm_unsupported {
    ($($arg:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Return an `Err(WasmError::Unsupported(msg))` where `msg` the string built by calling `format!`
on the arguments to this macro.

```
macro_rules! wasm_unsupported {
    ($($arg:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
Return an `Err(WasmError::Unsupported(msg))` where `msg` the string built by calling `format!`
on the arguments to this macro.

# ConstExpr in wasmtime_types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasmtime-types/25.0.3/wasmtime_types/struct.ConstExpr.html

`pub struct ConstExpr { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A constant expression.

These are used to initialize globals, table elements, etc…

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasmtime_types/lib.rs.html#1399-1403)#### pub fn [new](https://docs.rs#method.new)(ops: impl [IntoIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.IntoIterator.html)<Item = [ConstOp](https://docs.rs/enum.ConstOp.html)>) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasmtime_types/lib.rs.html#1399-1403)

#### pub fn [new](https://docs.rs#method.new)(ops: impl [IntoIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.IntoIterator.html)<Item = [ConstOp](https://docs.rs/enum.ConstOp.html)>) -> Self

Create a new const expression from the given opcodes.

Does not do any validation that the const expression is well-typed.

Panics if given zero opcodes.

Create a new const expression from a `wasmparser` const expression.

Returns the new const expression as well as the escaping function
indices that appeared in `ref.func` instructions, if any.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasmtime_types/lib.rs.html#1454-1471)#### pub fn [provably_nonzero_i32](https://docs.rs#method.provably_nonzero_i32)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasmtime_types/lib.rs.html#1454-1471)

#### pub fn [provably_nonzero_i32](https://docs.rs#method.provably_nonzero_i32)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.bool.html)

Is this ConstExpr a provably nonzero integer value?

This must be conservative: if the expression *might* be zero,
it must return `false`. It is always allowed to return `false`
for some expression kind that we don’t support. However, if it
returns `true`, the expression must be actually nonzero.

We use this for certain table optimizations that rely on knowing for sure that index 0 is not referenced.

# Global in wasmtime_types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasmtime-types/25.0.3/wasmtime_types/struct.Global.html

```
pub struct Global {
    pub wasm_ty:
```
[WasmValType](https://docs.rs/enum.WasmValType.html),
    pub mutability: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.bool.html),
}## Expand description

A WebAssembly global.

Note that we record both the original Wasm type and the Cranelift IR type
used to represent it. This is because multiple different kinds of Wasm types
might be represented with the same Cranelift IR type. For example, both a
Wasm `i64` and a `funcref` might be represented with a Cranelift `i64` on
64-bit architectures, and when GC is not required for func refs.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.wasm_ty)

`wasm_ty: `[WasmValType](https://docs.rs/enum.WasmValType.html)The Wasm type of the value stored in the global.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.mutability)

`mutability: `[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.bool.html)A flag indicating whether the value may change at runtime.

# Memory in wasmtime_types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasmtime-types/25.0.3/wasmtime_types/struct.Memory.html

```
pub struct Memory {
    pub minimum:
```
[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html),
    pub maximum: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html)>,
    pub shared: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.bool.html),
    pub memory64: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.bool.html),
    pub page_size_log2: [u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html),
}## Expand description

WebAssembly linear memory.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.minimum)

`minimum: `[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html)The minimum number of pages in the memory.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.maximum)

`maximum: `[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html)>The maximum number of pages in the memory.

Whether the memory may be shared between multiple threads.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.memory64)

`memory64: `[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.bool.html)Whether or not this is a 64-bit memory

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.page_size_log2)

`page_size_log2: `[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)The log2 of this memory’s page size, in bytes.

By default the page size is 64KiB (0x10000; 2**16; 1<<16; 65536) but the
custom-page-sizes proposal allows opting into a page size of `1`.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasmtime_types/lib.rs.html#1600-1604)#### pub fn [minimum_byte_size](https://docs.rs#method.minimum_byte_size)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html), [SizeOverflow](https://docs.rs/struct.SizeOverflow.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasmtime_types/lib.rs.html#1600-1604)

#### pub fn [minimum_byte_size](https://docs.rs#method.minimum_byte_size)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html), [SizeOverflow](https://docs.rs/struct.SizeOverflow.html)>

Returns the minimum size, in bytes, that this memory must be.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

Returns an error if the calculation of the minimum size overflows the
`u64` return type. This means that the memory can’t be allocated but
it’s deferred to the caller to how to deal with that.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasmtime_types/lib.rs.html#1620-1628)#### pub fn [maximum_byte_size](https://docs.rs#method.maximum_byte_size)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html), [SizeOverflow](https://docs.rs/struct.SizeOverflow.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasmtime_types/lib.rs.html#1620-1628)

#### pub fn [maximum_byte_size](https://docs.rs#method.maximum_byte_size)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html), [SizeOverflow](https://docs.rs/struct.SizeOverflow.html)>

Returns the maximum size, in bytes, that this memory is allowed to be.

Note that the return value here is not an `Option` despite the maximum
size of a linear memory being optional in wasm. If a maximum size
is not present in the memory’s type then a maximum size is selected for
it. For example the maximum size of a 32-bit memory is `1<<32`. The
maximum size of a 64-bit linear memory is chosen to be a value that
won’t ever be allowed at runtime.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-1)Errors

Returns an error if the calculation of the maximum size overflows the
`u64` return type. This means that the memory can’t be allocated but
it’s deferred to the caller to how to deal with that.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasmtime_types/lib.rs.html#1644-1657)#### pub fn [max_size_based_on_index_type](https://docs.rs#method.max_size_based_on_index_type)(&self) -> [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasmtime_types/lib.rs.html#1644-1657)

#### pub fn [max_size_based_on_index_type](https://docs.rs#method.max_size_based_on_index_type)(&self) -> [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html)

Returns the maximum size memory is allowed to be only based on the index type used by this memory.

For example 32-bit linear memories return `1<<32` from this method.

# ModuleInternedTypeIndex in wasmtime_types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasmtime-types/25.0.3/wasmtime_types/struct.ModuleInternedTypeIndex.html

`pub struct ModuleInternedTypeIndex(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

A canonicalized type index for a type within a single WebAssembly module.

Note that this is deduplicated only at the level of a single WebAssembly module, not at the level of a whole store or engine. This means that these indices are only unique within the context of a single Wasm module, and therefore are not suitable for runtime type checks (which, in general, may involve entities defined in different modules).

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

# RecGroupRelativeTypeIndex in wasmtime_types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasmtime-types/25.0.3/wasmtime_types/struct.RecGroupRelativeTypeIndex.html

`pub struct RecGroupRelativeTypeIndex(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

A canonicalized type index referencing a type within a single recursion group from another type within that same recursion group.

This is only suitable for use when hash consing and deduplicating rec groups.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

# StaticModuleIndex in wasmtime_types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasmtime-types/25.0.3/wasmtime_types/struct.StaticModuleIndex.html

`pub struct StaticModuleIndex(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

Index into the global list of modules found within an entire component.

Module translations are saved on the side to get fully compiled after the original component has finished being translated.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

# VMSharedTypeIndex in wasmtime_types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasmtime-types/25.0.3/wasmtime_types/struct.VMSharedTypeIndex.html

Struct VMSharedTypeIndex    Copy item path  Source  `pub struct VMSharedTypeIndex();`Expand description A canonicalized type index into an engine’s shared type registry.

This is canonicalized/deduped at the level of a whole engine, across all the
modules loaded into that engine, not just at the level of a single
particular module. This means that `VMSharedTypeIndex` is usable for
e.g. checking that function signatures match during an indirect call
(potentially to a function defined in a different module) at runtime.

Create a new instance from a `u32`.

Return the underlying index value as a `u32`.

`source`.
